title: Electrical power and energy — what it costs to run your devices
examTip: Multi-step calculation questions are common. Write down what you know and pick the right equation. Substitute carefully, and always include units. Practice is the only way to get fast at this.
introTips: Before you start: can you write down P = IV, E = Pt and V = IR from memory? If not, that is your first job.
Before reading, try estimating the power of five appliances at home. Then check how close you were.
Watch the unit conversions: watts ↔ kilowatts, seconds ↔ hours. These trip people up in exams.
intro: Every time you boil a kettle, stream a video or charge your phone, you pay for electrical energy. The bill at the end of the month comes straight from the physics you are about to learn. Power and energy are not just abstract maths. They tell you which appliances cost the most to run. They show why LED bulbs save money. They let you work out the exact cost of a tumble dryer cycle. These equations also come up in almost every electricity exam question.

keyPoints.heading: Electrical power
keyPoints.content: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred. It is how many joules are transferred per second. The unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. The key equations are: - P = IV (power = current × voltage) - P = I²R (put V = IR into P = IV) - P = V²/R (put I = V/R into P = IV) Worked example 1: a kettle with I = 10 A and V = 230 V → P = 10 × 230 = 2300 W = 2.3 kW. Worked example 2: a phone charger with I = 1 A, V = 5 V → P = 1 × 5 = 5 W. Worked example 3: a resistor with R = 20 Ω and I = 3 A → P = 3² × 20 = 9 × 20 = 180 W. Typical values to know: kettle ~2 kW, microwave ~800 W, laptop ~65 W, LED bulb ~10 W, old incandescent bulb ~60 W. 1 kW = 1000 W.
writeBullets: Power — the rate of energy transfer. Measured in watts (W). 1 W = 1 J/s
P = IV (the main equation: power = current × voltage)
P = I²R (substitute V = IR into P = IV)
P = V²/R (substitute I = V/R into P = IV)
Kettle: I = 10 A, V = 230 V → P = 2300 W = 2.3 kW
1 kW = 1000 W. Typical appliances: kettle 2 kW, LED bulb 10 W, laptop 65 W

keyTerms.def: The rate of energy transfer; measured in watts (W). P = IV.
The unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second.
1000 watts; used for higher-power appliances like kettles and heaters.

keyPoints.memTip: PIV: Power = I × V. Think of it as 'PIV-ot', the central equation everything else turns around.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often use P = IV and forget P = I²R. Use P = I²R when the voltage is not given. All three equations are the same equation in different forms. There is no new physics, just algebra.

keyPoints.heading: Electrical energy
keyPoints.content: Energy transferred = power × time: E = Pt. The units are joules (J) when P is in watts (W) and t is in seconds (s). Putting in P = IV gives E = IVt. Worked example 1: a 2 kW kettle running for 3 minutes → E = 2000 × (3 × 60) = 2000 × 180 = 360,000 J = 360 kJ. Worked example 2: a 60 W bulb left on for 1 hour → E = 60 × 3600 = 216,000 J = 216 kJ. For bills, electricity companies use a much larger unit: the kilowatt-hour (kWh). 1 kWh = the energy transferred by a 1 kW device running for 1 hour = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3,600,000 J = 3.6 MJ. Units used (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours). Worked example 3: a 2 kW kettle for 30 minutes = 2 kW × 0.5 h = 1 kWh.
writeBullets: E = Pt (energy = power × time). Joules when P is in W and t in seconds
E = IVt (substitute P = IV)
Always convert time to seconds before using joules
kWh: the energy unit for bills. 1 kWh = energy from a 1 kW device for 1 hour
Units used (kWh) = Power (kW) × time (hours)

keyTerms.def: The total energy moved from one store to another; E = Pt (joules) or Power (kW) × time (hours) for kWh.
The unit electricity companies use for billing; the energy transferred by a 1 kW device in 1 hour = 3.6 MJ.
The SI unit of energy; 1 J = 1 W × 1 s.

keyPoints.memTip: Joules = watts × seconds (small scale). kWh = kilowatts × hours (big scale, for bills). The physics is the same. The units just suit different situations.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Know when to use seconds (for joules) and when to use hours (for kWh). Mixing them up is the most common mistake in energy calculations.

keyPoints.heading: Cost of electricity
keyPoints.content: Once you know how many kilowatt-hours an appliance uses, you can work out the cost. Cost = units used (kWh) × price per unit (p/kWh). The exam question gives you the price per kWh. A typical value is around 28p per kWh. This varies, so always use the figure given. Worked example 1: a 2.5 kW tumble dryer runs for 2 hours → units = 2.5 × 2 = 5 kWh → cost = 5 × 28p = 140p = £1.40. Worked example 2: a 100 W television watched for 4 hours → units = 0.1 kW × 4 h = 0.4 kWh → cost = 0.4 × 28p = 11.2p. Ways to save energy: - switch to LED bulbs (10 W vs 60 W incandescent for the same light) - turn devices off standby - take shorter showers (if you use an electric shower) - use appliances at off-peak times Payback time = extra cost of the efficient appliance ÷ yearly saving. Example: an energy-efficient boiler costs £800 more but saves £200/year → payback time = 800 ÷ 200 = 4 years. After 4 years it starts saving money.
writeBullets: Cost (pence) = units (kWh) × price per kWh (p)
Units used (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours). Convert watts to kilowatts first
Worked example: 2.5 kW dryer × 2 h = 5 kWh × 28p = £1.40
Payback time = extra upfront cost ÷ annual saving (in years)
LED bulbs: ~10 W vs 60 W incandescent. Same light, 83% less energy
The price per kWh is always given in the exam. Don't learn a fixed value

keyTerms.def: Cost (p) = units used (kWh) × price per unit (p/kWh). Units = power (kW) × time (hours).
The time it takes for savings from an energy-efficient appliance to recoup the extra purchase cost. Payback time = extra cost ÷ annual saving.
Using less energy to achieve the same output; e.g. LED bulbs give the same light as incandescent bulbs for a fraction of the power.

keyPoints.memTip: Units → cost: power (kW) × hours = kWh. kWh × pence = pence. Always do it in that order and you won't go wrong.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A common slip is forgetting to convert watts to kilowatts before working out kWh. That gives answers 1000× too large. Make a habit of writing 'P = ___ W = ___ kW' before every calculation.

keyPoints.heading: Linking all the electrical equations
keyPoints.content: In a multi-step calculation, you need to choose and combine equations. Here is how they all link together: - V = IR (Ohm's Law: voltage = current × resistance) - P = IV (power). Substituting gives P = I²R and P = V²/R - E = Pt (energy = power × time). Substituting gives E = IVt - Q = It (charge = current × time; Q in coulombs, C) - E = QV (energy = charge × voltage). This links the mechanical 'work done' idea of energy to circuit quantities Multi-step strategy: (1) write down all the values you know (2) find what the question asks for (3) choose the equation that links what you know to what you need (4) substitute values (5) rearrange if needed (6) check units Worked multi-step example: a resistor has R = 50 Ω and V = 10 V. Find the energy transferred in 2 minutes. Step 1: I = V/R = 10/50 = 0.2 A. Step 2: P = IV = 0.2 × 10 = 2 W. Step 3: E = Pt = 2 × 120 = 240 J.
writeBullets: V = IR — Ohm's Law. Links voltage, current and resistance
P = IV — power. Leads to P = I²R and P = V²/R by substitution
E = Pt = IVt — energy transferred, in joules
Q = It — charge (coulombs) = current × time
E = QV — energy = charge × voltage. Links work done to circuit quantities
Multi-step strategy: list knowns → pick equation → substitute → rearrange → check units

keyTerms.def: The quantity of electricity flowing past a point; Q = It. Unit: coulombs (C).
Energy transferred (J) = charge (C) × voltage (V). Connects the electrical quantities to the concept of work done.
A calculation requiring two or more equations applied in sequence.

keyPoints.memTip: Draw a spider diagram with P in the middle. Draw all four equations coming out from it: P=IV, P=I²R, P=V²/R, E=Pt. Then link V=IR as the bridge between them.
keyPoints.tutor_note: E = QV is often skipped, but it comes up in higher-grade questions. It is just energy = work done to move charge Q through a potential difference V. It is the same idea as W = Fd, but for electrical charge.

tables.title: Typical power values of common appliances

0.question: A hairdryer has a resistance of 23 Ω and draws a current of 10 A. What is its power?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! P = I²R = 10² × 23 = 100 × 23 = 2300 W = 2.3 kW. This is the right equation when you have current and resistance but not voltage.
0.wrongFeedback: Use P = I²R. Square the current first (10² = 100), then multiply by resistance (100 × 23 = 2300 W). P = IV would also work. First find V = IR = 10 × 23 = 230 V, then P = 10 × 230 = 2300 W.

1.question: A 3 kW electric heater runs for 2.5 hours. How many kWh does it use? What does it cost at 28p per kWh?
1.correctFeedback: Perfect. Units = 3 kW × 2.5 h = 7.5 kWh. Cost = 7.5 × 28p = 210p = £2.10. Clean two-step calculation.
1.wrongFeedback: Step 1: Units (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours) = 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 kWh. Step 2: Cost = 7.5 kWh × 28p = 210p = £2.10.

2.question: A resistor has R = 50 Ω and V = 10 V. What is the energy transferred in 2 minutes?
2.correctFeedback: Correct! First find P = V²/R = 100/50 = 2 W. Then E = Pt = 2 × 120 = 240 J. (Remember: 2 minutes = 120 seconds.)
2.wrongFeedback: This is a multi-step calculation. Step 1: P = V²/R = 10²/50 = 100/50 = 2 W. Step 2: convert 2 minutes to seconds (× 60) = 120 s. Step 3: E = Pt = 2 × 120 = 240 J.

3.question: An energy-efficient washing machine costs £150 more than a standard model. It saves £50 per year on electricity bills. What is the payback time?
3.correctFeedback: Right. Payback time = extra cost ÷ annual saving = £150 ÷ £50 = 3 years. After that, the savings are pure profit.
3.wrongFeedback: Payback time = extra cost ÷ annual saving = 150 ÷ 50 = 3 years. Don't mix up the numbers. Divide the upfront cost by the yearly saving.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert watts to kilowatts before working out kWh. Divide by 1000. A 2000 W kettle is 2 kW, not 2000 kW.
Using seconds instead of hours (or the other way round) when working out energy. Use seconds for joules (E = Pt) and hours for kWh. Mixing them up gives wildly wrong answers.
Using P = I + V, or some made-up equation, instead of P = IV. Power is a product (multiplication), not a sum.
Forgetting to square the current in P = I²R. Writing P = IR instead of P = I²R gives the voltage, not the power.
Leaving units out of answers. Mark schemes need the correct unit (W, J, kWh) as well as the number.
examTips: In multi-step electricity calculations, always write out every step. Examiners give marks for correct working, even if your final answer is wrong. Never skip steps.
The price per kWh is always given in the exam question. Never learn a fixed value. Read the question carefully and use the number given.
When a question gives you R and I, use P = I²R straight away. Don't work out V first and then use P = IV. It is faster and gives fewer chances for arithmetic slips.
